record_reviews.summary: Darwin writes from the Beagle after leaving England, gives a compressed voyage narrative from St Jago to Bahia and Rio, and describes collecting marine animals, fresh-water beetles, spiders and geological specimens. The letter is also intensely personal: Cambridge memories and the long separation from Fox occupy the later blocks. It is a complete six-block outgoing letter from May 1832, not an answer to a scientific question.

evidence.quote: We sailed from England after much difficulty on the 27th of December
I am entirely occupied with land animals

record_reviews.summary: Darwin acknowledges a long silence, reports receiving letters after four months at Montevideo, and worries about Fox’s health. He then describes South American natural history, extinct-animal remains, Buenos Aires and the return voyage, asks Fox to write again, and credits Henslow with receiving specimens. The shipboard travel and social material are intertwined; no discrete scientific prompt is answered.

evidence.quote: At M: Video we had not heard from anybody for four month
I hope you will write to me again

record_reviews.summary: Darwin says two Fox letters dated August and January reached him after a Tierra del Fuego cruise. He contrasts Cambridge friendship with shipboard life, discusses the unproductive East-coast cruise, geology and the voyage route, and explicitly says Fox’s question about his ornithology has helped him watch birds. This is a substantive travel response with multiple incoming letters.

evidence.quote: I received your two letters dated at the wide of interval of August & January
Your question: what I did in Ornithology? has done me good

record_reviews.summary: Darwin writes before another long Beagle interval, describing the overland journey from the Río Negro through Bahia Blanca and Santa Fe, geology of fossil-bearing beds and danger from Indians and settlers. He says letters will not be exchanged for six or eight months and hopes to find Fox’s at Valparaiso. It is a farewell/travel update rather than an answer to a preserved question.

evidence.quote: We shall not receive or write letters for the next six or eight months
We shall in a week leave for ever the muddy estuary of the Plata

record_reviews.summary: Darwin congratulates Fox on marriage, sets out the Beagle’s planned route through the Galapagos and Pacific, reports Pselaphidae and the Concepción earthquake, and explains plans to cross the Cordillera. He asks Fox for news and leaves the letter open in case another arrives. The correspondence is explicitly interrupted by illness and voyage logistics.

evidence.quote: I have heard nothing about you for a long time
I will keep this letter open for the chance of receiving one from you

record_reviews.summary: Darwin says Fox’s June and November 1834 letters arrived in inverted order and thanks him for the personal news. He describes the long voyage, hopes to return to Fox’s fireside, explains his geological work from Peru to Copiapó and the Galapagos route, and asks Fox to write to the Cape of Good Hope. The arrival statement identifies a real incoming sequence, but only the November endpoint is in this packet.

evidence.quote: I have lately received two of your letters, one dated June & the other November 1834
I am become a zealous disciple of Mr Lyells views

record_reviews.summary: At Sydney Darwin records the disappointment of finding no letter because the Beagle arrived early, and says the last home news concerned Mrs Fox’s ill health. He describes the chronometrical phase of the voyage, loneliness and the anticipated return, then turns to sentimental travel writing. No Fox prompt is answered because no letter arrived.

evidence.quote: we all on board the Beagle were bitterly disappointed in not finding a single letter
there will be then a space of 18 months

record_reviews.summary: Fox writes after learning from Darwin’s sister that Darwin had been heard from. He apologizes for a delayed, deliberately uneventful letter, gives domestic news and hopes Darwin will return safely. It is social correspondence from 30 June 1832, with no substantive scientific question.

evidence.quote: I commenced a letter at the time but was prevented finishing it
that I may again see you in health & happiness in Old England

record_reviews.summary: Fox’s multipart letter begins with relief at receiving Darwin’s hand, then records illness and dated continuations on 18 and 28 September. He reports his own walks, insects and Colias on the island, repeatedly postpones dispatch, and closes warmly. The internal dates show composition over weeks, not a single-day message.

evidence.quote: I had hoped to have heard a few lines from you in the last 5 months
I have much enjoyed seeing our Navy

record_reviews.summary: Fox writes to reach Darwin at Valparaiso after obtaining the address from Caroline, gives extensive family, health and marriage news, reports travel in a pony carriage, and asks where Darwin is and how the South Sea voyage is going. He explicitly refers to an earlier April letter from the Falklands and Jemmy Button, so this is an incoming social letter with multiple remembered communications.
